The Business Mindset

Before you buy any stock, you need a clear picture of how a business actually makes money. This module explains revenue, costs and profit in plain terms, shows how owners think about risk and decisions, and helps you find a real opportunity and shape it into a one-page business concept.

A business is any regular activity where you offer something people want, they pay you for it, and after paying all your costs, money is left over. That leftover money is **profit**. A woman who buys a bag of rice in bulk and sells it in cups near her house is running a business. So is a tailor, a hairdresser, a caterer or a woman who sells recharge cards. Size does not decide whether it is a business. The habit of earning more than you spend, again and again, does.
A woman standing at a small shop counter with goods on shelves
A small shop is a business when what customers pay is more than what the goods and running costs cost the owner.
Where the value comes from

Customers do not pay you for nothing. They pay because you save them something: time, effort, transport, or worry. A woman who sells provisions on her street saves her neighbours a trip to the big market. A caterer saves a family the stress of cooking for 100 guests. This is called **creating value**. When you understand the value you give, you understand why people will pay you, and how much they may be willing to pay.
**Convenience:** you are close, open when needed, or you deliver.
**Quantity that fits:** you break a big pack into sizes people can afford, such as selling rice by the cup or detergent by the sachet.
**Skill:** you can do something they cannot, such as sewing, baking or braiding.
**Trust and quality:** your goods are genuine, fresh and correctly measured.

Busy is not the same as profitable

A stall can be full of customers and still lose money. This happens when the selling price is too close to the buying price, when goods spoil or get stolen, when the owner gives too much credit, or when transport and levies eat up the small gain on each item. In this course you will learn to check each of these. The first step is simple: always ask, 'After everything, what did I keep?'
Do not count stock money as profit
If you take money from the business for personal needs, write it down as money taken out. Otherwise you will think the business is doing well when it is actually being eaten up.

There are three common kinds of small business. **Trading** means buying goods and selling them at a higher price without changing them, like selling provisions or fabrics. **Production** means turning materials into a new product, like making soap, chin chin or zobo. **Services** means selling your skill or time, like hair, tailoring or phone repairs. Many women combine them: a tailor sells her sewing service and also sells fabric. Most of this course uses trading examples because they are the easiest way to see buying price, selling price and profit clearly, but the same rules apply to every kind.

One more idea will help you all through this course: **capital**. Capital is the money and things you put into the business to make it run, such as cash for stock, a table, a cooler or a sewing machine. Your aim is for the business to protect its capital and slowly add to it from profit. If, after three months, you have less stock and less cash than when you started, the business is losing capital, even if you were busy every day. Check this at the end of each month by counting your stock at cost price and adding the business cash you have.

Two women can sell the same goods in the same market and get very different results. Often the difference is not luck or capital. It is how they think. An **owner** treats the business as something separate from herself that she must feed, protect and grow. A person who only **sells** treats the money as household money and the stall as a way to get cash today. This lesson is about the owner's habits.

Five habits of an owner
**She knows her numbers.** She can tell you roughly what she sold this week and what she kept.
**She pays herself on purpose.** She takes a fixed amount for personal needs, not whatever is in the purse.
**She protects her capital.** Money for stock is not touched for anything else.
**She is consistent.** Her customers know when she opens and what she sells.
**She learns.** When something goes wrong, she asks why and changes one thing.
Every decision has a gain, a cost and a risk

Before spending business money, an owner asks three questions. What will this bring me (the **gain**)? What will it cost me, in money and time (the **cost**)? What could go wrong, and how bad would it be (the **risk**)? Risk is not something to fear. It is something to measure and reduce. Starting with small quantities, testing before buying in bulk, and keeping some money aside are all ways to reduce risk.
Worked example: should she buy a whole bag?

Risk: she sells about 5 kg a day, so the bag would last about 10 days. Rice stored dry and off the floor keeps well over that time, so spoilage risk is low.
Risk two: spending ₦85,000 leaves only ₦15,000 for her other goods for 10 days.

Set your own rules

Owners write simple rules and keep them, especially on hard days. Rules protect you from pressure by relatives, friends and customers. Here are examples many small traders use. Choose the ones that fit you and write them in your notebook.
I will not use stock money for personal needs. If I must, I write it down and repay it.
I will pay myself a fixed amount each week, for example ₦10,000, only from profit.
I will give credit only to customers who have paid before, with a limit, for example ₦3,000, and a date to pay.
I will open at the same time every day I trade.
I will count my money and write my sales before I go to bed.
Saying no politely

When someone asks for goods on credit you cannot afford, try: 'My sister, this money is not mine, it belongs to the business. I can keep this one for you until you come with the money.' It protects the friendship and your stock.
Learn from mistakes quickly

Every trader makes mistakes: buying goods that do not sell, trusting the wrong customer, pricing too low. The owner's habit is a short weekly review. Ask: What went well? What went badly? What will I change next week? Change one thing at a time so you can see whether it worked. A notebook with three lines each Sunday is enough.

Finally, an owner manages her time as carefully as her money. If your business shares the day with children, a job or house work, decide your trading hours and protect them. A shop that opens at different times every day trains customers to go elsewhere.

Owners also guard against the biggest money risks in small trading: theft, fake notes, failed transfers and fraud. Keep cash out of sight and bank it or move it to a business account often. Before you release goods for a transfer, confirm the money has actually arrived in your account or POS app, not just that the customer shows you a screenshot or an SMS. Fake credit alerts are a known trick, so check your own app or balance every time.

Good business ideas usually come from paying attention, not from a sudden flash. Look at what people around you complain about, what they travel far to buy, what is often sold out, and what they pay for every week. Each of these is a clue to an **opportunity**: a need that is not yet well served, which you could serve at a profit.
A woman with a lightbulb above her head
Opportunities often start as everyday complaints you hear in your street or market.
Where to look
**Complaints:** 'There is nowhere to buy bread after 7pm here.' 'The tailor never finishes on time.'
**Distance:** people take a bus to buy basic items you could sell closer to them.
**Repeat needs:** things families buy every week such as food items, toiletries, airtime, cooking gas refills.
**Seasons and events:** school resumption, festive periods, rainy season, weddings and naming ceremonies.
**New places:** a new estate, school, hospital or construction site creates new customers.
Check demand before you spend

An idea is only an opportunity if enough people want it **and can pay** a price that gives you profit. Test cheaply first. Count how many people pass a spot at the time you would trade. Ask ten possible customers what they buy now, where, and at what price. Watch whether similar sellers nearby are busy. Then sell a small quantity, for example one carton, and see how fast it goes.
Ask about the past, not the future
People are kind and will often say 'Yes, I will buy' to a new idea. A better question is 'When did you last buy this, and how much did you pay?' Real past buying tells you more than polite promises.
Compare your ideas with a simple score

Write down three ideas and score each one from 1 (poor) to 5 (strong) on four points: demand (do many people need it often?), start cost (5 means cheap to start), your skill or knowledge, and competition (5 means few sellers nearby). Add the scores. The highest total is usually the best first business, though you should still test it small.

She tests snacks first with about ₦25,000 of stock, keeping the rest as a reserve.

Traps to avoid
**Copying the crowd:** if ten women already sell the same thing in one line, the price war leaves little profit. Find a different spot, product or service such as delivery.
**Following hype:** a product trending on social media may not sell in your area.

**Ignoring rules:** some goods need approval or care. Packaged food, drinks, cosmetics and drugs are regulated by NAFDAC; selling drugs needs a licence. Start with goods you can sell legally and safely.
**Big first orders:** never put all your capital into one untested product.

Your own strengths matter too. If you are known for cooking, people already trust your food. If you have many friends in a church or association, you have a ready first market. An opportunity you can serve with skills and relationships you already have carries less risk than one you must learn from zero.
Look at the whole chain, not only selling

Sometimes the best opportunity is not selling the main product but serving the people who sell it. Around any busy market you will find openings in supply, transport and support: delivering goods to shops, selling packaging such as nylon bags and food containers to food sellers, selling ice or cold water to traders on hot days, or offering POS cash withdrawal where there is no bank nearby. These businesses often face less direct competition because fewer people notice them.

When you notice an opening, write it down the same day with three facts: who has the need, how often they need it, and what they use now. A list of twenty such notes over two weeks gives you far better choices than one idea you have been dreaming about for years. Keep the list in your notebook or in a WhatsApp chat with yourself so you can come back to it when you are ready to start or add a new line.

An idea such as 'I want to sell food' is too vague to act on. A **business concept** is the same idea made specific: who you will serve, exactly what you will sell, at what price, where, and how people will hear about you. You can fit it on one page. This page becomes your guide for buying stock and talking to customers, and the starting point for any plan or loan application later.

For a first business, choose products that are bought often, are not too expensive for your customers, do not spoil fast, and that you can buy reliably from a nearby supplier. Fast-moving everyday goods such as provisions, toiletries, grains and drinks suit beginners because you learn quickly from many small sales. Goods that spoil quickly, like fresh fish or tomatoes, can give good margins but need fast selling and careful handling.

The five parts of a concept
**Customer:** who exactly will buy? For example, 'workers at the Ogba bus stop between 6am and 9am.'
**Offer:** what you sell and why it is better or easier. 'Hot akara and pap, wrapped clean, served fast.'
**Price:** what customers pay and what it costs you. 'Akara ₦100 a piece, costs me about ₦60.'
**Place:** where and when you trade. 'Beside the junction, 6am to 9:30am, Monday to Saturday.'
**Promotion:** how people will know. 'A clean signboard, a WhatsApp status each morning, a free piece for every tenth purchase.'

Be honest with your estimates
New owners usually guess sales too high and costs too low. Use the lowest sales number you think is likely, and add a little extra to costs for transport, losses and levies.
What to test in your first two weeks

Decide in advance what you want to learn. How many units do you really sell each day? Which items sell fastest and which sit? Do customers complain about price? What time of day is busiest? Write the answers every evening. After two weeks, update your one-page concept with real numbers. You will use this page again in the next module when we look at start-up costs, customers and pricing in more detail.
Find your difference

Your concept should answer one more question: why would a customer buy from you and not from the next seller? You do not need something new to the world. A small, clear difference is enough. Examples include being open earlier or later than others, keeping goods cold when others sell them warm, selling in smaller sizes, packaging food more neatly, offering delivery within your estate, or giving correct change every time. Write your difference in one line at the top of your concept page.

Finally, think about who you will buy from. Note two or three possible suppliers, their location, their prices and whether they sell in the quantities you need. Big markets such as Mile 12 and Idumota in Lagos, Ariaria in Aba, Onitsha Main Market or Kano's Kurmi and Singer markets are known wholesale centres, but a nearby distributor may be cheaper once you count transport and your time. Having more than one supplier protects you when one runs out or raises prices.

This module turns your concept into a business you can open. You will list what you truly need to start, get to know your customers and choose a good trading spot, set prices that leave real profit using gross profit, markup and margin, and understand which registrations apply to a small Nigerian business.

Many women delay starting because they believe they need a shop, a big signboard and a full stock. Most successful small businesses started much smaller. What you need is enough to serve your first customers well, plus a small reserve for surprises. Everything else can come later from profit. This approach is called a **lean start**: spend as little as possible until real sales show you what is worth buying.
A woman reviewing a budget on a large calculator
A start-up budget shows exactly where your first money goes before you spend it.
The three parts of start-up money
**Equipment and fixed items:** things you buy once and use for a long time, such as a table, umbrella, cooler, scale, shelves or a sewing machine.
**First stock:** the goods you will sell in your first one to two weeks.
**Cash reserve:** money kept aside for restocking, small repairs, levies and slow days. A useful rule is to keep at least two weeks of running costs in reserve.
Must-have or nice-to-have?

For every item on your list, ask: 'Can I serve my first customers without this?' If yes, it is nice-to-have and can wait. A rented shop may be nice-to-have if you can start from a table at your gate or a shared stall. A big signboard can wait; a neat handwritten board works at first. A cooler may be a must-have if you sell drinks in the heat, because customers want them cold.

How much first stock?

Buy small quantities of many fast items rather than large quantities of a few. Your first weeks are for learning what your customers actually buy. Ask suppliers which items sell fastest. Buy enough of each to last about one to two weeks, then restock what sold and drop what did not. Empty spaces can be filled with your best sellers.
Ways to start with less

Share a stall or a bulk purchase with a trusted trader. Buy used equipment in good condition. Ask your supplier whether you can pay part now and part on delivery once trust is built. Start with pre-orders, for example collecting orders for a product on WhatsApp before you buy it.
Where the start-up money comes from

Most small businesses in Nigeria start with personal savings, contributions from an ajo or esusu group, or support from family. Be careful with loans at the very start: a loan must be repaid even if sales are slow, and interest adds to your costs. It is usually safer to start small with your own money, prove that the business makes profit, then borrow to grow. Module 4 covers finance options in detail.

Whatever the source, write down where each naira came from. If a relative gives you ₦50,000, agree clearly whether it is a gift or a loan, and if it is a loan, when and how you will repay it. Many family quarrels start from unclear money. A short written note signed by both of you is enough.
Plan your stock list from your concept

Turn your first stock money into a written list before you go to market. For each item write the quantity, the expected buying price and the planned selling price. Total the list and compare it with your budget. If it is too high, cut slow or expensive items first, not your best sellers. At the market, write the real prices beside your estimates; you will use these real numbers in the pricing lesson. Never go to the wholesale market with all your money and no list, because it is easy to be persuaded to buy things that do not suit your customers.

Knowing your customers and choosing your location

Every business decision gets easier when you know exactly who buys from you. What you stock, how you price, where you stand and how you advertise all depend on your customer. 'Everybody' is not a customer group. 'Mothers in my estate who buy food items for the week on Saturday mornings' is.
A target with a group of people at its centre
The clearer your picture of the customer, the easier every other choice becomes.
Describe your customer
**Who:** workers, students, mothers, artisans, traders, drivers.
**Where:** where they live, work or pass each day.
**When:** the days and hours they buy.
**What and how much:** the items, the sizes and how much they usually spend at once.
**How they pay:** cash, transfer, POS or credit.
**What they care about:** lowest price, freshness, speed, trust, delivery.
Learn by watching and asking

You do not need a big survey. Stand near your planned spot at the hours you would trade and count how many people pass in 30 minutes. Note who they are. Watch nearby sellers: which items do people buy most, and what do they ask for that is not available? Then talk to ten people. Ask what they buy, how often, where, and at what price. Write the answers in your notebook. This is real **market research**.
Listen for the words 'I wish'
When customers say 'I wish you had...' or 'Do you sell...?', write it down. Five people asking for the same thing is a strong signal to stock it.
Choosing a location

For a trading business, location often matters more than anything else. A good spot has many of your kind of customer passing at the right time, is easy to see and reach, is safe, and has costs that your profit can carry. A cheap spot with no customers is not cheap. Before you agree to rent, visit at different times and days.
Worked example: comparing two spots
For example, Esther sells snacks and drinks and must choose between two spots in Abuja. Figures are illustrative and approximate.
Spot A, inside a quiet estate: about 40 people pass in 30 minutes at evening rush. Rent about ₦10,000 a month.
Spot B, beside a busy bus stop: about 150 people pass in 30 minutes at morning and evening rush. Rent about ₦30,000 a month.
From her test days she expects about 1 in 20 people passing to buy, spending about ₦500.
Spot A: 40 ÷ 20 = 2 buyers per half hour. Over 4 busy hours that is about 16 buyers, or ₦8,000 in sales a day.
Spot B: 150 ÷ 20 = 7 or 8 buyers per half hour, about 60 buyers over 4 busy hours, or ₦30,000 in sales a day.
The extra ₦20,000 rent at Spot B is about ₦770 per day over 26 trading days, far less than the extra sales.
Spot B costs more but is likely to give much higher profit. Esther chooses Spot B and confirms with the landlord and the local market or council authority what levies apply.

Match your hours to your customers

Workers buy early morning and evening. Mothers often shop on weekend mornings. Students buy at break and after school. If you sell near a church or mosque, days of worship may be your busiest. Be open when your customers buy, and be consistent so they can rely on you. If you can only trade part of the day because of children or a job, choose the hours with the most buyers rather than spreading yourself thin across the whole day. Two strong hours at the right time can bring more sales than six quiet ones.
Safety and rules at your location

Ask about the rules before you set up. Many markets and local government areas charge daily or monthly levies, and some roadsides are not allowed for trading. Ask the market association or the local government office what is permitted, and keep receipts for any levy you pay. Avoid spots under electric cables, too close to fast traffic, or where water collects in the rainy season. Your safety and your stock come first.

Your customers will change over time, and so should your picture of them. Every month, look back at your sales notes. Which items sold most, on which days, and to whom? Which customers came back again and again? Pricing for profit: cost price, gross profit, markup and margin
Work out the full cost price of an item, including transport and packaging
Calculate gross profit, markup and gross margin
Set a selling price from a target margin
Check a price against customers and competitors

Pricing is where many small businesses quietly lose money. A price that is too low makes you busy but poor. A price that is too high sends customers to the next stall. This lesson gives you the numbers to price with confidence. You need four terms: **cost price**, **selling price**, **gross profit** and the difference between **markup** and **margin**.
A price tag
Every price tag should be backed by a calculation of cost and profit.
Step 1: find the true cost price
The cost price of one item is not just what you paid the supplier. Add the transport to bring the goods, and any packaging. Divide by the number of units. This is your **landed cost** per unit.
Worked example: landed cost of noodles
For example, Kemi buys instant noodles by the carton in Lagos and sells single packs. Figures are illustrative and approximate; use your own supplier's prices.
One carton of 40 packs costs her about ₦9,600 at the wholesale market.
She buys 5 cartons (₦48,000) and pays ₦2,000 for transport, which is ₦400 per carton.
Landed cost per carton: ₦9,600 + ₦400 = ₦10,000.
Landed cost per pack: ₦10,000 ÷ 40 = ₦250.
She plans to sell each pack at ₦300.
Kemi's true cost is ₦250 per pack, not ₦240. Forgetting transport would have made her think she earns ₦60 per pack when she really earns ₦50.
Step 2: gross profit, markup and margin
Term
Formula
Kemi's noodles
Gross profit per unit
Selling price minus cost price
Markup
Gross profit ÷ cost price × 100
Gross margin
Gross profit ÷ selling price × 100

Markup and margin describe the same ₦50, measured against different numbers. **Markup** compares profit with what you paid. **Margin** compares profit with what the customer paid. Margin is always the smaller percentage. The danger is mixing them up: if you want a 30% margin but you add 30% to cost, you only get about 23% margin.
Markup versus margin
Margin
Profit divided by cost
Always the bigger percentage
Easy for setting prices
Profit divided by selling price
Always the smaller percentage
Shows share of each sale kept
The same naira profit gives a bigger markup percentage than margin percentage.
Step 3: set a price from a target margin
If you know the margin you want, use this formula: **Selling price = cost price ÷ (1 minus target margin)**. Write the margin as a decimal, so 25% is 0.25.
Worked example: pricing a bucket of garri
For example, Ifeoma sells garri in 4 litre paint buckets in Owerri. Figures are illustrative and approximate.
Her landed cost for one bucket is about ₦2,400, including transport.
She wants a 25% gross margin.
Check: gross profit = ₦3,200 minus ₦2,400 = ₦800. Margin = ₦800 ÷ ₦3,200 = 25%. Markup = ₦800 ÷ ₦2,400 = about 33%.
She sees nearby sellers charge between ₦3,000 and ₦3,300, so ₦3,200 fits the market.
Ifeoma prices at ₦3,200 and knows exactly why. If competitors were at ₦2,800, she would need a cheaper supplier, not a lower margin.
Step 4: check against the market
**Your floor:** never go below landed cost plus a share of your running costs, or every sale loses money.
**The market:** what similar sellers nearby charge for the same quality.
**Your value:** cold drinks, delivery, cleaner packaging or a better location can justify a slightly higher price.
**Round sensibly:** prices like ₦300 or ₦3,200 make change easier and reduce mistakes.
Gross profit is not your final profit

Gross profit only removes the cost of the goods. Rent, levies, phone data, bags and your own pay still have to come out of it. A business can have a healthy gross margin and still make a loss if running costs are too high.

When supplier prices rise, update your prices quickly. Write each item's landed cost and selling price in your notebook and check them every time you restock. In a period of rising prices, selling today at yesterday's price can mean you cannot afford to buy the same quantity again.
Pricing services and made goods

The same method works if you sell a service or make a product. Add up the materials used for one unit, for example thread, buttons and lining for one dress, or flour, oil, sugar and packaging for one bag of chin chin. Add a fair amount for your time and a share of costs such as gas or electricity. That total is your cost per unit. Then apply your target margin. Women who sell their skill often forget to count their own hours, so they work very hard and earn little. If a dress takes you six hours, your price must reward those hours, not just cover the fabric.
Landed cost includes the supplier price, transport and packaging.
Gross profit = selling price minus cost price.
Markup divides profit by cost; margin divides profit by selling price.
Selling price = cost ÷ (1 minus target margin).

Many small traders in Nigeria operate without formal registration, especially when starting. Registration is not the first thing you need to make profit, but it becomes important as you grow: to open a business bank account in the business name, to supply larger customers, to apply for some loans and grants, and to protect your business name. This lesson explains the main registrations so you know what applies to you and when.
An identity card
Registration links your business name to you and your identity documents.
The Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)

The **CAC** is the government agency that registers businesses in Nigeria. A sole trader usually registers a **business name**. This is the simplest form: you trade under a name such as 'Mama Ada Provisions', and you personally own the business and are personally responsible for its debts. A **limited company** (Ltd) is a separate legal body with its own responsibilities; it costs more to set up and maintain and suits larger businesses. Most women starting a small trade begin with a business name.

Main steps to register a business name

Registration is done online through the CAC portal, which you reach from the official website, cac.gov.ng. The process can change, so always follow the current instructions on that site. In general, the steps are:
Create an account on the CAC online portal using your email address.
Search for and reserve your proposed business name. Have two or three options ready in case the first is taken.
Fill in the registration form: your details, business address and the nature of your business.
Upload the required documents, such as a valid means of identification, passport photograph and signature, as the portal requests.
Pay the official fee online. Check the current fee on the CAC website.
Download your certificate and registration documents once approved.
Beware of fake agents

Only pay official fees on the CAC portal itself. If you use an agent, use an accredited one you can verify, ask for a receipt, and insist that the registration is in your own name with your own email so you control the account.

Register in stages as your business grows; product approvals depend on what you sell.
Product rules: NAFDAC and SON

If you only **resell** goods made by others, your main duty is to sell genuine, safe, in-date products. Check that packaged food, drinks, cosmetics and medicines carry a NAFDAC registration number, and do not sell expired or tampered goods. If you **make or package** food, drinks, cosmetics or similar products yourself for sale, **NAFDAC** (the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control) regulates them, and you will need to look into its registration requirements; NAFDAC has guidance for small producers on its website. **SON** (the Standards Organisation of Nigeria) sets standards for many manufactured products.

Toyin runs a growing supply business and wants contracts with companies. She registers a business name now and plans to consider a limited company as contracts grow.
Each woman's needs depend on what she does: reselling, producing, or supplying larger buyers.
Tax and local levies

Businesses in Nigeria can obtain a Tax Identification Number (TIN), which banks and larger customers often ask for. Local governments and markets also charge levies and permits. Tax rules for small businesses have been changing, so check current guidance from the Federal Inland Revenue Service or your state revenue service, or ask a trusted accountant, rather than relying on hearsay. Keep receipts for every levy and fee you pay; your records from Module 3 will make any tax conversation much easier.

Registration does not make an unprofitable business profitable. Get your product, customers and pricing right first, then register when it helps you grow. But do not wait too long: once people know your business name, register it so nobody else can.

Running Your Business Day to Day

Once you are open, profit is won or lost in daily habits. This module covers buying and rotating stock and measuring how fast it sells, serving customers so they return, keeping business money separate and recorded in a simple book, and setting goals you can check every month.
Managing stock: buying, rotating and measuring stock turnover
Keep a simple stock list and count stock regularly
Use first in, first out to reduce spoilage and expiry
Calculate stock turnover and days of stock
Decide when and how much to reorder

For a trader, stock is money sitting on a shelf. Every carton that does not sell is cash you cannot use. Every item that expires or gets damaged is money lost. Good stock management means having enough of what customers want, not too much of what they do not, and knowing exactly what you have.
A cardboard box of goods
Each box on your shelf is cash waiting to be turned back into money.
Keep a stock list and count often

Write every item you sell in your notebook with its cost price. Once a week, on the same day, count how many of each item you have. Multiply by the cost price and add up. That total is your **stock value at cost**. When you compare it with your purchases and sales, you can spot losses from theft, spoilage or mistakes early.

First in, first out (FIFO)

When new stock arrives, put it **behind** the old stock so the older items sell first. This is called **first in, first out**. It matters most for food, drinks, cosmetics and anything with an expiry date. Check expiry dates when you buy and refuse goods that are close to expiry unless the supplier gives a real discount and you know you can sell them in time. Never sell expired or damaged goods; it can harm customers and destroys trust.
Store goods safely

Keep food items off the floor, away from damp, direct sun, rats and chemicals. Store kerosene, insecticides and detergents separately from food. Keep goods dry in the rainy season with pallets or crates under them.
Stock turnover: how fast your money comes back

**Stock turnover** tells you how many times in a period you sell through your average stock. A higher turnover means your money comes back faster and you can buy again more often. The formula is: **Stock turnover = cost of goods sold in the period ÷ average stock value at cost**. Average stock is the opening stock plus closing stock, divided by 2. You can also find **days of stock**: the number of days in the period divided by the turnover.
Worked example: one month of stock turnover
For example, Patience runs a provisions stall in Benin City. Figures are illustrative and approximate.
Stock value at cost on 1 March: ₦80,000. On 31 March: ₦70,000.
Cost of goods she sold in March, from her records: ₦300,000.
Stock turnover = ₦300,000 ÷ ₦75,000 = 4 times in the month.
Days of stock = 31 ÷ 4 = about 8 days. On average, goods sit on her table for about 8 days before selling.

Patience's money comes back about four times a month. When she checks item by item, she finds one brand of cooking oil has sat for over a month, so she stops reordering it and puts that money into faster items.

Display, oldest in front
Sell and record
Count weekly
Reorder fast sellers
Each turn of this cycle brings your cash back; the faster it turns, the more you can earn on the same money.
When and how much to reorder
**Know your daily sales** of each item from your record book.
**Know your delivery time:** how many days between deciding to buy and having the goods on your table.
**Reorder level:** daily sales × delivery days, plus a small safety stock. If you sell 10 packs a day, restock every 3 days, and keep 10 packs extra, reorder when you are down to 40 packs.
**Order quantity:** enough for your normal buying cycle, for example one week, not more than you can sell before goods expire or your cash runs short.
Slow sellers and dead stock

Items that sit for weeks tie up your money. Sell them off with a small discount, bundle them with fast items, or return them to the supplier if allowed. Then do not reorder. It is better to have a smaller range of goods that move than a crowded table of goods that sit. Use your weekly count to mark items that have not sold at all.

Finally, protect your stock from losses. Count cash and stock at the same time each week. If someone helps you at the stall, give them a starting count and check it when they hand over. Most losses are small leaks: a few items given to family, a few taken by visitors, a few broken. Written counts make these leaks visible so you can stop them.

Seasons change what sells. Before school resumption, festive periods or the rainy season, look at what sold last year at the same time and buy a little extra of those items early, while prices are often lower. After the season, return to normal quantities quickly so you are not left holding items nobody wants until next year.

Customer service that brings people back
Describe the service habits that make customers return

Finding a new customer costs time and effort. Keeping one costs much less. A regular customer who buys from you twice a week for a year is worth far more than a stranger who buys once. In small trading, where many sellers offer the same goods at similar prices, **service** is often the main reason a customer chooses you.
A smiling customer receiving goods from a seller
Customers come back to sellers who treat them well and keep their word.
Service habits that work
**Greet every customer** warmly and use their name when you know it.
**Be honest about quality:** if tomatoes are soft today, say so. Customers remember honesty.
**Give correct measures and change.** Use a proper scale or measure and count change in front of the customer.
**Keep your space clean and goods neat.** People judge food and toiletries by how they are displayed.
**Be reliable:** open at the same times and keep your best sellers in stock.
**Keep promises:** if you say you will keep an item or deliver at 5pm, do it, or call before the time.
Handling complaints
Complaints are a chance to win a customer for life. Most unhappy customers never complain; they simply stop coming. The ones who complain are giving you a chance to fix it. Use four steps.
**Listen fully** without interrupting or arguing.
**Acknowledge and apologise:** 'I am sorry this happened. Thank you for telling me.'
**Fix it fairly:** replace the item, refund, or offer something that matches the problem.
**Prevent it next time:** find out why it happened and change something.

For example, a regular customer returns to Mercy's stall in Jos saying a tin of milk was spoiled when opened.
Mercy listens and checks the tin. The expiry date is fine, but the tin is dented.
She apologises and replaces the tin at once, at a cost to her of about ₦1,500 (approximate).

She adds a new rule: check every tin for dents and swelling when stock arrives.
Mercy spends about ₦1,500 to keep a customer who spends several thousand naira with her every week, and her new check prevents the same problem.
Credit: the silent business killer

Selling on credit (allowing customers to pay later) can bring loyalty, but unpaid credit is one of the most common reasons small businesses collapse. Money owed to you is not money you can use to restock. If you give credit, make the rules clear and write everything down.
Give credit only to regular customers with a history of paying.
Set a limit per person, for example ₦3,000, and a payment date.
Write each credit sale in a credit page: name, phone number, date, items, amount, date paid.
Do not give new credit until the old balance is paid.
Keep total credit to a small share of your stock, so one bad debt cannot sink you.
Make it easy to pay

Accepting bank transfers and POS or app payments through providers such as Moniepoint, OPay or Paystack can make it easier for customers to pay on the spot and to clear credit. Always confirm the money has arrived in your own account before handing over goods.
Keep a regular customer list

Write down your regular customers' names, phone numbers (with their permission), what they usually buy and any preferences. You can then tell them when their favourite item arrives, remember them on special days, and notice when someone stops coming so you can check on them. Protect this information: do not share customers' numbers with others or add them to groups without asking.

Little extras build loyalty at low cost: a small 'dash' for a regular, a free nylon bag, carrying heavy items to a car, or keeping an item aside for someone. Count these as part of your marketing costs, and keep them small and steady so customers value them without expecting more each time.
Service on the phone and WhatsApp

More and more customers order by phone or WhatsApp before they come. Reply quickly, even if only to say 'I have seen your message, I will confirm in ten minutes.' Give the full price including any delivery charge before the customer pays, so there are no surprises. Send a short message when the order is ready or on its way. If an item is out of stock, say so honestly and suggest a close alternative or the date it will arrive. Customers forgive a delay much more easily than silence. Treat a customer who messages at night with the same respect as one at your table, but it is fine to set and share your business hours.

Separating business and personal money, and keeping simple records

Record daily sales, purchases and expenses in a simple book

Understand cash flow and why profit and cash are not the same

The habit that most often decides whether a small business survives is simple: **keep business money and personal money apart**. When school fees, food and family needs are paid straight from the stall's cash, stock money disappears and the owner cannot tell whether the business is making profit or not.
An open record book
A simple record book tells you what you sold, what you spent and what you kept.
How to separate the money
**Use a separate place for business money:** a separate purse or box at first, and later a separate bank or mobile money account for the business.
**Pay yourself a fixed amount** from profit, for example weekly. Move it from the business to your personal purse or account on the same day each week.
**Record anything else you take** as 'owner drawings', including goods taken for home use.
**Never pay personal costs directly from the business.** Pay yourself first, then pay personal costs from your own money.
A second account helps

Many banks and mobile money providers let you open a second account. Using one only for the business makes it easy to see what came in and went out. Once you register a business name, you can open an account in that name.
The simple record book

You need only a notebook or a simple spreadsheet on your phone. Each day, write the date, and under it: money in (sales, split into cash and transfer if you like), money out for stock (purchases), money out for other costs (transport, levy, bags, data), and money you took for yourself. At the end of the day, count your cash and check your account balance. They should match what your book says.

Working out monthly profit

Profit for a month is **sales minus cost of goods sold minus running costs**. Cost of goods sold is not the same as what you bought, because some goods you bought are still on the shelf. Use your stock counts: **Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases minus closing stock**, all at cost price. Your own weekly pay is not a business cost here; it comes out of the profit.
Worked example: a month's profit and margin
For example, Joy sells provisions in Warri and keeps a record book. Figures are illustrative and approximate.
Sales for June: ₦380,000.
Opening stock 1 June: ₦70,000. Purchases in June: ₦300,000. Closing stock 30 June: ₦75,000.
Gross profit = ₦380,000 minus ₦295,000 = ₦85,000. Gross margin = ₦85,000 ÷ ₦380,000 = about 22%.
Running costs: transport ₦12,000, levies ₦3,000, bags ₦4,000, phone data ₦3,000. Total ₦22,000.
Joy paid herself ₦40,000 during the month, so ₦23,000 stays in the business to grow it.
Joy knows her business made about ₦63,000 in June and that her personal pay is affordable. Without the book she would only have guessed.

Each step removes a cost; what remains at the end is what the business truly earned.
Profit is not the same as cash

**Cash flow** is the movement of money in and out over time. A profitable business can still run out of cash if money is tied up in stock or unpaid credit, or if a big purchase falls in the same week as rent. Look ahead each month: list the big payments coming (rent, school fees from your personal pay, bulk stock) and make sure enough cash will be there. Keep your cash reserve topped up.

Records also protect you. They show a lender or cooperative that your business is real and profitable, help you answer tax questions, and settle disagreements with partners or family. Keep receipts from suppliers in an envelope or photograph them on your phone each day.
When the book and the cash do not match

Some days your counted cash and account balance will not match the book. Do not ignore the gap. Check, in this order: a sale or expense you forgot to write; a transfer that has not yet arrived or was reversed; change given wrongly; money taken for home use without recording it; and finally, loss or theft. Write the difference as 'unexplained' so you can see whether it happens often. A small gap once in a while is normal. A gap every week is a warning that you need to tighten how cash is handled, especially if someone else helps you sell.

Simple business planning and goal setting

A plan does not need to be long. For a small business, a clear goal, a few numbers, and a monthly check against your records are enough to keep you moving forward. Without goals, months pass and the business stays the same size. With goals, you know what to aim for each day.
A woman reaching a target on a goals board
Clear goals turn hope into daily targets you can track.
SMART goals

A well-known way to write goals is the **SMART** method. A SMART goal is **Specific** (exactly what), **Measurable** (a number you can check), **Achievable** (realistic for your capital and time), **Relevant** (it matters to your business), and **Time-bound** (it has a date).
Weak goal
SMART goal
I want to grow my business
Increase weekly sales from about ₦80,000 to ₦100,000 by 31 March
I will save more
Move ₦5,000 of profit into a business savings account every Saturday for 12 weeks
I want more customers
Add 20 regular customers to my list by the end of next month
From a profit goal to a daily target

Work backwards from what you want to earn. Start with your target net profit for the month, add your running costs, and divide by your gross margin to find the sales you need. Then divide by trading days.
Worked example: what must she sell each day?
For example, Lami sells foodstuffs in Kano. She wants to make ₦90,000 net profit a month. Figures are illustrative and approximate.
Her running costs are about ₦25,000 a month. So she needs gross profit of ₦90,000 + ₦25,000 = ₦115,000.
Her gross margin, from her records, is about 20% (0.20).
Sales needed = ₦115,000 ÷ 0.20 = ₦575,000 a month.
She trades 26 days a month: ₦575,000 ÷ 26 = about ₦22,100 a day.
Her current sales are about ₦17,000 a day, so she needs about ₦5,100 more each day.
Lami now has a clear daily target. She plans two actions: adding a fast-moving product her customers ask for, and opening an hour earlier for morning buyers.
A simple planning rhythm
Daily: record sales
Weekly: count stock
Monthly: profit review
Quarterly: set new goals
Small regular checks keep your plan connected to what is really happening.
The monthly review
Set aside one hour at the end of each month. Use your record book to answer these questions and write the answers on one page.
What were my total sales, gross profit and net profit?
Did I reach my goals? If not, why not?
Which items sold best and which were slow?
How much credit is owed to me, and by whom?
Is my business capital (stock plus business cash) higher or lower than last month?
What one or two things will I change next month?
Be kind but honest with yourself
A month below target is information, not failure. Look for the cause in your numbers: lower sales, lower margin, higher costs, or money taken out. Then change one thing.
A one-page business plan

Combine your concept from Module 1 with real numbers. A one-page plan has: your business name and what you sell; your customers and location; your prices and gross margin; your monthly sales, costs and profit (actual and target); your goals for the next three to six months; and what you need (money, equipment, skills) to reach them. This page is useful when you approach a cooperative, microfinance bank or grant programme, and it reminds you what you are working towards.

Plans change, and that is fine. A sudden price rise, a new competitor or a road closure can change your numbers. When something big changes, redo your daily target with the new figures. The habit of planning matters more than any single plan being perfect.
Three ways to raise profit

When you plan how to reach a profit goal, remember there are only a few levers to pull. You can **sell more** (more customers, more items per customer, more trading hours). You can **earn more per sale** (better buying prices, a slightly higher price where your value allows it, or adding higher-margin items). Or you can **spend less** on running costs (combining market trips, buying bags in bulk, cutting waste and spoilage). Small changes in each can add up.

For example, if a trader raises sales by 10%, cuts her buying cost by buying with a neighbour in bulk, and reduces spoilage, her profit can grow much more than 10%, because her running costs stay about the same while gross profit rises. Use your monthly review to test one lever at a time, so you can see which one works best for your business. Write the result next to the goal it was meant to help.

Finally, plan for the unexpected. Set aside a small part of profit every month into a reserve until it covers at least one month of running costs. This reserve is what carries you through illness, a family emergency, a market closure or a sudden price jump without having to sell off stock cheaply or borrow at high interest.
Write goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

Marketing your business on a small budget

Marketing is everything you do to make the right people know about your business, want what you sell, and choose you. It is not only advertising. Your display, your prices, your location, how you greet people and what customers say about you are all marketing. Most small businesses grow mainly through word of mouth, and the good news is that word of mouth can be encouraged on a very small budget.
A megaphone
Simple, steady messages to the right people beat expensive one-off adverts.
The four Ps
A widely used way to think about marketing is the **four Ps**. You already met each of them in this course; marketing means making them work together.

Low-cost ways to promote
**A clear sign and display:** a clean, readable sign with your name and what you sell; goods arranged neatly, best sellers in front, prices visible.
**Samples and tasting:** for food items, a small free taste can sell more than any poster.
**Referrals:** reward customers who bring new buyers.
**Your existing networks:** church, mosque, association, school parents and workplace groups, used politely and not too often.
**Partnerships:** a hairdresser can recommend your hair products; a caterer can buy your drinks; you recommend each other.
**WhatsApp status and catalogue:** covered fully in the next lesson.
Your brand is your reputation
A brand is simply what people think and say when they hear your business name. A consistent name, a clean look and reliable service build a brand at almost no cost.
Worked example: is a referral offer worth it?
For example, Yetunde sells foodstuffs in Abeokuta. She offers any customer who brings a new customer a free 1 kg of beans, which costs her about ₦1,500 (approximate).
A new regular customer spends about ₦6,000 a week with her, at a gross margin of about 20%, so about ₦1,200 gross profit a week.
The referral reward costs ₦1,500 once.
If the new customer stays for just two weeks, Yetunde earns ₦2,400 gross profit, more than the reward.
In one month, eight customers bring a friend. Five of the new customers keep buying.
Rewards cost 8 × ₦1,500 = ₦12,000. Five new regulars add about 5 × ₦1,200 = ₦6,000 gross profit per week.
The offer pays for itself in about two weeks and keeps adding profit afterwards. Yetunde counts the cost in her records as a marketing expense.

Measure what works

Before you spend on any marketing, decide how you will know if it worked. Ask new customers, 'How did you hear about us?' and tally the answers in your notebook. Compare sales in the week before and the week after a promotion. Use a different code or phrase for each method, for example 'Mention STATUS for a free sachet', so you know which channel brought the customer. Stop what does not work and repeat what does.
Discounts: use with care

A discount comes straight out of your gross profit. If your margin is 20% and you give 10% off, you have lost half your profit on that sale. Use discounts for a clear purpose, such as clearing slow stock, rewarding bulk buyers, or bringing first-time customers, and for a short time. A free extra item that costs you little, such as a sachet of seasoning with a bag of rice, often feels more generous to the customer while costing you less than a price cut.

Finally, keep promises in your marketing. If your sign says 'Always fresh', never sell stale goods. If your status says 'Delivery in 1 hour', deliver in an hour. Marketing brings customers once; only honest delivery brings them back.
Plan around the calendar

Many sales peaks are predictable. School resumption, Ramadan and Sallah, Easter, Christmas and New Year, and local festivals all change what people buy. Write the main dates for your area in your notebook and plan a simple promotion two weeks before each one: stock up on the items that sell at that time, tell your customers early on WhatsApp and with your sign, and consider gift packs or bundles. A provisions seller might offer a festive pack of rice, oil, tomato paste and seasoning at one rounded price. Work out the pack's cost first so the bundle price still leaves your normal margin.

Safety, scams and privacy
Confirm every payment yourself

Never release goods because of a screenshot, a forwarded SMS or a 'transfer receipt'. Check that the money has arrived in your own bank or payment app. Fake alerts and fake receipts are common tricks.
Never share your bank PIN, OTP codes, BVN details or your WhatsApp verification code with anyone, even if they say they are from your bank or WhatsApp.

Add people to broadcast lists or groups only with their permission. Broadcast messages only reach people who have saved your number.
Do not post customers' names, phone numbers or addresses publicly.

Social media works best as a steady habit. A few clear posts every day, quick replies and honest delivery will grow trust over months. If you later move to Facebook or Instagram, the same rules apply: clear photos, prices, proof and fast replies.
Taking good product photos with your phone

Good photos sell. You do not need an expensive phone. Take photos in daylight near a window or outside in shade, not under harsh midday sun or at night with flash. Use a plain background such as a white wall, a clean cloth or a tray. Wipe the camera lens first. Show the product clearly and, where it helps, show size by placing it beside a common object or in someone's hand. Take several shots and post only the clearest. Keep the same style for all your products so your catalogue looks neat and trustworthy.

Think about data too. Many of your customers pay for every megabyte. Short, clear photos and short videos are kinder to them than long videos. Put the price and key details in the caption so customers can decide without asking and waiting for a reply.

Know the true cost of a loan

Lenders describe interest in different ways, so always ask: **'How much will I repay in total, including every fee, and how much each week or month?'** Get the answer in writing. A rate 'per month' is very different from a rate 'per year'. Interest charged 'flat' on the whole amount costs more than it sounds, because you pay interest on money you have already repaid.
Worked example: can she afford this loan?
For example, Hauwa is offered a ₦200,000 loan from a microfinance bank in Minna to buy stock in bulk. The terms below are illustrative; real terms vary by lender.
Interest: 5% flat per month for 6 months. 5% of ₦200,000 = ₦10,000 per month, so ₦60,000 in interest over 6 months.
Processing fee: 2% of the loan = ₦4,000, taken at the start, so she receives ₦196,000.
Total repayment: ₦200,000 + ₦60,000 = ₦260,000, or about ₦43,300 per month. Of this, about ₦33,300 returns the loan itself and ₦10,000 is interest.
Total cost of borrowing: ₦60,000 + ₦4,000 = ₦64,000, or about ₦10,700 a month on average.
From her records, she expects the bulk stock (cheaper buying price plus more sales) to add about ₦12,000 a month to her net profit.
Gain after the loan's cost: ₦12,000 minus ₦10,700 = only about ₦1,300 a month.
Because she must hand back about ₦33,300 of the loan every month, her extra stock shrinks as she repays, so the real gain is likely smaller still, and a slow month would turn it into a loss.
The loan would cost Hauwa almost everything it earns, with real risk. She decides to save through her cooperative for three months and then borrow a smaller amount from it at lower cost.

Good and bad reasons to borrow

Borrow for things that bring money back quickly and reliably, such as bulk stock you already sell fast at a good margin. Avoid borrowing to cover losses, for personal spending, or for a new idea you have not tested. If the business is losing money, a loan only makes the loss bigger.
Cooperatives and savings groups

Cooperatives and rotating savings groups are among the most common ways Nigerian women raise business capital. They build discipline, and cooperatives can offer loans at lower cost to members. Join a group whose members you know, whose rules are written, and whose records are kept and shared. Ask how long members have been receiving their payouts on time.
Grants and support programmes

Some organisations run programmes with training and funding for small businesses. Examples include the Tony Elumelu Foundation Entrepreneurship Programme, which accepts applications from African entrepreneurs, and the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN), which provides support and information for small businesses. Programmes open and close at different times, so check their official websites directly. A good one-page business plan and clear records from Module 3 make your application stronger.
Spot finance scams

Real grants never ask you to pay a fee to receive the money. Be suspicious of messages promising quick grants or loans if you pay 'processing' or 'registration' fees first, of lenders who want your phone contacts, and of anyone asking for your BVN, PIN or OTP. Check that a lender is licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria, and for loan apps, check the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) list of approved digital lenders.

Reinvest from profit, step by step

A simple rule many owners use is to split each month's net profit into three parts: your personal pay, a reserve, and money to grow the business. The exact split is yours to decide, but write it down and keep to it. Growth money then builds steadily without starving your household or your reserve.
Worked example: growing in steps
For example, Comfort sells provisions in Calabar and makes about ₦80,000 net profit a month. Figures are illustrative and approximate.
She splits profit: ₦40,000 personal pay, ₦15,000 reserve, ₦25,000 growth money.

Protect the business as it grows
**Do not depend on one supplier:** keep at least two for your main items.
**Do not depend on one big customer:** if one buyer is most of your sales, losing them hurts badly.
**Control credit:** growing sales to other traders on credit can drain your cash fast.
**Protect cash and stock:** bank cash often, lock stock, and keep counts.
**Train and check helpers:** give clear instructions, written stock counts at handover and fair pay.
**Keep records up to date:** bigger businesses hide losses more easily.
Growth also means growing you

Think long term

Long-term success comes from many small good habits repeated for years: knowing your numbers, treating customers well, paying yourself fairly, saving a reserve and growing only from strength. Every six months, look back at your capital (stock plus business cash) and compare it with six months earlier. If it is growing while you pay yourself, your business is healthy. Write a short plan for the next six months with one or two growth goals, and begin again.

Remember that growth is a choice, not a duty. Some owners choose a steady, well-run business that supports their family comfortably. Others aim to build something much larger. Both are valid. What matters is that you decide on purpose, with your numbers in front of you, rather than drifting.

As the business grows, revisit the registrations from Module 2. A bigger business may need a business name or company registration, a business bank account, a Tax Identification Number and, if you start producing or packaging goods yourself, the right product approvals. Getting these in place before a big opportunity arrives, such as a supply contract with a school or company, means you can say yes when it comes.

Profit = sales minus all costs = ₦40,000 minus (₦31,000 + ₦1,500) = ₦7,500.
Which is the strongest sign that an idea has real demand?
Friends say they like the idea
People can tell you when they last bought it and what they paid

Nobody else sells it anywhere
Past buying is real evidence of demand; polite approval is not.

Only the product and its price

A carton of 20 items costs ₦8,000 and transport for it is ₦400. You sell each item at ₦500. What is your gross margin?
Landed cost = ₦8,400 ÷ 20 = ₦420. Gross profit = ₦80. Margin = 80 ÷ 500 = 16%.
Your landed cost is ₦900 and you want a 25% gross margin. What selling price should you set?
Selling price = cost ÷ (1 minus 0.25) = ₦900 ÷ 0.75 = ₦1,200. Adding 25% to cost (₦1,125) would give only a 20% margin.

Turnover = 150,000 ÷ 50,000 = 3 times. Days of stock = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 days.

Argue that it was fine when sold

Sales, costs and profit: thinking like an owner
Sales, costs and profit: thinking like an owner.
This is the video for module one of Introduction to Small Business and Trading.
Why this matters
Know how your business makes money
Customers pay for value
Profit is not the cash in your purse
Owners weigh gain, cost and risk
Test ideas small before you spend

A business is any regular activity where people pay you for something they want, and after all your costs, money is left over. Customers pay because you save them time, effort, transport or worry. That is called creating value.
Many new traders look at the money in their hand and call it profit. It is not. Most of it belongs to your stock.
You will learn to think like an owner, who weighs every spend before she makes it.
And you will learn to find a real opportunity and test it cheaply.
Three words
Sales, costs and profit
Sales: all the money customers pay you
Costs: goods, transport, rent, levies, packaging
Profit: sales minus all costs
Three words every owner must know. Sales, also called revenue, is all the money customers pay you.
Costs are everything you spend to make those sales: the goods, transport, rent, levies and packaging.
Profit is sales minus all costs. Always ask yourself, after everything, what did I keep?
Worked example
One day at a provisions table
For example, Bisi sells drinks, biscuits and noodles from a table in Ibadan.
Cost of the goods she sold
Keke from the market
Nylon bags
Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.
Here is a worked example. Bisi sells drinks, biscuits and noodles from a table in front of her house in Ibadan. Today her sales add up to about 18,000 naira.
Now her costs. The goods she sold cost her about 14,400 naira in cartons. She paid 800 naira for a keke from the market, and 200 naira for nylon bags.
Total costs, 15,400 naira. So her profit is 18,000 minus 15,400, about 2,600 naira.
She has 18,000 naira in her purse, but only about 2,600 is profit. The 14,400 must go back into stock, or her table will be empty within a week.
Owner or seller?
Habits that grow a business
An owner
Knows her numbers
Pays herself a fixed amount
Protects stock money
Reviews every week
Only a seller
Guesses what she kept
Takes whatever is in the purse
Spends stock money at home
Repeats the same mistakes

An owner treats the business as separate from herself. She knows her numbers, pays herself a fixed amount from profit, never touches stock money, and every Sunday asks what went well, what went badly, and what she will change.
A person who only sells treats the money as household money. If stock money goes on food, school fees or a party, the business shrinks without her noticing.
If you must take money out, write it down.
Gain, cost, risk
Measure risk. Never put all your capital into one untested product.
Chioma sells rice by the cup in Enugu. A trader offers her a 50 kg bag cheaper. The gain is about 200 naira per kg, or about 10,000 naira on the bag.
The cost is about 85,000 naira at once, and she has 100,000 in business savings.
What could go wrong? Rice stored dry keeps well, so spoilage risk is low.
But spending 85,000 would leave only 15,000 naira for her other goods. So she starts smaller: she shares a bag with a trader she trusts, 25 kg each.
She still saves about 5,000 naira and keeps cash for her other goods. She measured the risk instead of guessing.
Protect your money
Three owner's rules
Only to customers who paid before, with a limit, for example ₦3,000, and a date.
Keep cash hidden and bank it or move it to a business account often.
Confirm money has arrived in your own account or POS app. Fake alerts are a known trick.
Owners write simple rules and keep them. Give credit only to customers who have paid before, with a limit, for example 3,000 naira, and a date to pay.
Keep cash out of sight, and bank it or move it to a business account often.
Before you release goods for a transfer, check your own app or balance. A screenshot or an SMS is not proof, because fake credit alerts are a known trick.
Spot an opportunity
Test demand before you spend
Listen to complaints and repeat needs
Ask: when did you last buy, and what did you pay?
Score ideas: demand, start cost, skill, competition
Sell a small quantity first

Opportunities hide in complaints, in things people travel far for, and in what families buy every week. Ask people when they last bought, and what they paid, because real past buying tells you more than polite promises.
Halima in Kaduna scored three ideas out of 5. Snacks at the school gate scored 15, the highest, so she tested it with about 25,000 naira of stock and kept the rest as a reserve.
Key points
Remember
Profit is sales minus all costs
Stock money goes back into stock first
Weigh gain, cost and risk
Check transfers in your own app
Test small before you commit

To remember. Profit is sales minus all costs, not the cash in your purse. Stock money goes back into stock first. Weigh gain, cost and risk before you spend. Check every transfer in your own app. And test small before you commit your capital.

Open small, price right, grow from profit
Start with what serves your first customers
Choose a spot by sales, not rent alone
Find your true cost before you price
Register when it helps you grow
Many women delay starting because they think they need a shop and a full stock. Most successful small businesses started much smaller. This is called a lean start.
Location often matters more than anything else, and a cheap spot with no customers is not cheap.
Pricing is where many small businesses quietly lose money. Too low makes you busy but poor.
And you will see which registrations apply to you, and when.
Worked example
A lean start-up budget
For example, Grace sells toiletries from a stall at her street junction in Port Harcourt.
Table, crates, umbrella, notebook
First stock: 12 fast items
Two weeks of running costs
Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.
Here is a worked example. Grace wants to sell soap, detergent, toothpaste and sanitary pads from a stall at her street junction in Port Harcourt.
Start-up money has three parts: equipment, first stock, and a cash reserve.
Equipment: a wooden table, crates, an umbrella, a notebook and calculator. About 43,000 naira.
First stock: 12 fast-moving items in small quantities, about 70,000 naira. Small amounts of many fast items teach her what customers really buy.

Spot A: estate

Esther sells snacks and drinks in Abuja. She counts passers-by. At Spot A, in a quiet estate, about 40 people pass in 30 minutes. Rent is about 10,000 naira a month, and she expects about 8,000 naira in sales a day.

At Spot B, beside a busy bus stop, about 150 pass. Rent is about 30,000 naira, but sales could reach about 30,000 naira a day. The extra rent is about 770 naira a day, far less than the extra sales. She chooses Spot B, and checks what levies apply.
Step by step
Find your true cost: Kemi's noodles
Landed cost = supplier price + transport + packaging.
Carton of 40 packs: about ₦9,600
Transport ₦2,000 for 5 cartons: ₦400 each
Landed cost per carton: ₦10,000
Sell at ₦300: gross profit ₦50
Kemi buys instant noodles by the carton in Lagos and sells single packs. One carton of 40 packs costs about 9,600 naira.
She buys 5 cartons and pays 2,000 naira for transport. That is 400 naira per carton.
So her landed cost per carton is 9,600 plus 400, which is 10,000 naira.
Divide by 40 packs. Her true cost is 250 naira a pack, not 240.
She sells at 300 naira, so gross profit is 50 naira a pack. Forgetting transport would have made her think she earns 60.
Markup and margin
Same profit, measured two ways
Markup: profit ÷ cost price × 100
Kemi: ₦50 ÷ ₦250 = 20% markup
Margin: profit ÷ selling price × 100
Margin is always the smaller percentage
Markup compares profit with what you paid. For Kemi, 50 divided by 250 is a 20 percent markup.
Margin compares profit with what the customer paid, so it is always the smaller percentage.
The danger is mixing them up. If you want a 30 percent margin but only add 30 percent to cost, you get less margin than you planned.
Price from a target
Ifeoma prices a bucket of garri
Selling price = cost ÷ (1 minus target margin)
Landed cost: about ₦2,400
Target margin 25%, written 0.25
Check nearby sellers: ₦3,000 to ₦3,300
If you know the margin you want, use this formula. Selling price equals cost divided by 1 minus your target margin.
Ifeoma sells garri in buckets in Owerri. Her landed cost is about 2,400 naira.
She wants a 25 percent margin. As a decimal, that is 0.25.
1 minus 0.25 is 0.75. And 2,400 divided by 0.75 is 3,200 naira. Her gross profit is 800 naira.
Nearby sellers charge between 3,000 and 3,300 naira, so her price fits the market.
Remember, gross profit is not final profit. Rent, levies, bags and your own pay still come out of it. And when supplier prices rise, update your prices quickly.
Rules that apply
Registration and product safety
Most traders start with a CAC business name
Pay fees only on the official CAC portal
Resellers: check NAFDAC numbers and expiry
Producers: look into NAFDAC requirements
Keep receipts for every levy
Most small traders register a business name with the CAC, online through cac.gov.ng. Pay official fees only on the portal, and keep the account in your own name, because fake agents exist.
If you resell, check NAFDAC numbers and expiry dates, and never sell expired goods. If you make or package food or cosmetics, look into NAFDAC requirements. And keep receipts for every levy.
Key points
Remember
Equipment, first stock and a cash reserve
Judge a spot by sales minus costs
Landed cost includes transport
Price = cost ÷ (1 minus target margin)
To remember. Budget for equipment, first stock and a cash reserve. Judge a spot by sales minus costs. Include transport in landed cost. Price from your target margin. Register when it helps you grow.

Daily habits: stock, customers, records and profit
Daily habits: stock, customers, records and profit.
This is the video for module three of Introduction to Small Business and Trading.
Why this matters
Profit is won or lost in daily habits
Stock is money sitting on a shelf
Keeping a customer costs less than finding one
Business money and home money apart
A simple book shows your real profit
Once you are open, profit is won or lost in daily habits. For a trader, stock is money sitting on a shelf. Every carton that does not sell is cash you cannot use.
A regular customer who buys twice a week for a year is worth far more than a stranger who buys once.
The habit that most often decides whether a small business survives is simple: keep business money and personal money apart.
And a simple record book shows what you really made.
Managing stock
Count, rotate and reorder
Never sell expired or damaged goods.
Count stock weekly, same day, at cost price
First in, first out: new stock behind old
Check expiry dates when you buy
Store food off the floor, away from chemicals
Drop slow sellers; reorder fast ones
Once a week, on the same day, count every item and multiply by its cost price. That total is your stock value at cost, and it shows up losses from theft, spoilage or mistakes early.
When new stock arrives, put it behind the old, so older items sell first. This is called first in, first out.
Check expiry dates when you buy, and refuse goods close to expiry unless you know you can sell them in time.
Keep food off the floor, away from damp, sun and rats. Store kerosene, insecticides and detergents separately from food.
Patience in Benin City found one brand of cooking oil had sat for over a month. She stopped reordering it and put that money into faster items.
And never sell expired or damaged goods. It can harm customers and destroys trust.
Customers who return
Service and credit
Do
Correct measures and change
Listen, apologise, fix, prevent
Credit only to regulars, written down
Avoid
Hiding soft or damaged goods
Arguing with a complaint
New credit before old is paid

Be honest about quality, and count change in front of the customer. When Mercy in Jos sold a dented tin of milk, she listened, apologised, replaced it at once, and now checks every tin when stock arrives.
Give credit only to regulars, with a limit, for example 3,000 naira, a date, and a written credit page.
Unpaid credit is one of the most common reasons small businesses collapse. Money owed to you cannot restock your table. So give no new credit until the old balance is paid.
Step by step
Separate the money
Pay yourself first, then pay personal costs from your own money.
A separate purse, box or account for the business
Pay yourself a fixed amount from profit
Write down anything else you take
Never pay home costs straight from the stall
Step one. Keep business money in its own place: a separate purse or box at first, and later a separate bank or mobile money account.
Step two. Pay yourself a fixed amount from profit, on the same day each week.
Step three. Record anything else you take as owner drawings, including goods taken home.
Step four. Never pay school fees or food straight from the stall's cash. Each day, write sales, stock bought, other costs and what you took. Then count your cash. It should match your book.
Worked example
Joy's profit for June
For example, Joy sells provisions in Warri and keeps a record book.
Transport
Levies
Bags
Phone data
Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.
Here is a worked example. Joy's sales for June are 380,000 naira.
Cost of goods sold is opening stock, plus purchases, minus closing stock. For Joy that is 70,000 plus 300,000 minus 75,000, which is 295,000 naira.
So her gross profit is 380,000 minus 295,000, which is 85,000 naira.
Now her running costs. Transport 12,000, levies 3,000, bags 4,000 and phone data 3,000 naira.
That is 22,000 naira. So her net profit is 85,000 minus 22,000, which is 63,000 naira.
She paid herself 40,000, so 23,000 stays in the business to grow it. Without the book, she would only have guessed.
Plan ahead
Goals and the monthly review
Profit is not cash: plan for big payments
Write SMART goals with a number and a date
Turn your profit goal into a daily target
Review one hour each month; change one thing
A profitable business can still run out of cash, if money is tied up in stock or credit, or a big purchase falls in the same week as rent. So look ahead each month.
Write goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. That is called SMART.
Lami in Kano wants 90,000 naira net profit a month. She works backwards and finds she needs about 22,100 naira of sales a day. Now she knows her target.
At the end of each month, spend one hour with your book. A month below target is information, not failure. Find the cause, and change one thing.
Key points
Remember
Count stock weekly; first in, first out
Credit only with limits, dates and records
Business money apart; fixed pay for you
Record every sale, cost and drawing
Review every month

To remember. Count stock weekly and sell the oldest first. Give credit only with limits, dates and records. Keep business money apart and pay yourself a fixed amount. Record every sale, cost and drawing. And review your numbers every month.
