Why this matters
Grow from strength, not from hope
Market on a small budget
Sell on WhatsApp, safely
Grow in tested steps from profit
With a profitable base and good records, you are ready to grow. Most small businesses grow through word of mouth, which costs very little.
WhatsApp is already the shop window for many Nigerian businesses.
Sooner or later you may need more money than profit gives. Every source has its own cost and risk.
And growing too fast is one of the main reasons small businesses fail. So you will learn to grow in steps.
Small-budget marketing
Promote without big spending
Clear sign, neat display, prices visible
Samples, referrals and partnerships
WhatsApp status: product, restock, tip
Ask: how did you hear about us?
Your display is marketing. Use a clean, readable sign, put best sellers in front, and show prices.

Yetunde in Abeokuta gives a free 1 kg of beans, costing her about 1,500 naira, to any customer who brings a new one. A new regular brings about 1,200 naira gross profit a week, so the reward pays for itself in about two weeks.
On WhatsApp Business, post clear daylight photos with the price, new restocks, and useful tips. Nneka in Onitsha posts three status updates each morning.
Then ask every new customer how they heard about you, and tally the answers. Repeat what works. And be careful with discounts, which come straight out of gross profit.
Selling safely
Protect your money online
Confirm every payment in your own app
Never share PIN, OTP, BVN or WhatsApp code
Turn on two-step verification
Add people to lists only with permission
Never release goods because of a screenshot, a forwarded SMS or a transfer receipt. Check your own bank or payment app. Fake alerts are common tricks.

Never share your bank PIN, OTP, BVN details or WhatsApp code, even with someone who says they are from your bank. Turn on two-step verification. And add people to broadcast lists only with their permission.
True cost of a loan
Can Hauwa afford this loan?
Ask: how much will I repay in total, including every fee?
Loan ₦200,000 at 5% flat per month, 6 months
Interest ₦60,000; processing fee ₦4,000
Total cost of borrowing: ₦64,000
Extra profit expected: about ₦12,000 a month
Gain after cost: only about ₦1,300 a month
Hauwa in Minna is offered a 200,000 naira loan from a microfinance bank to buy stock in bulk. Interest is 5 percent flat per month for 6 months.
5 percent of 200,000 is 10,000 naira a month, so 60,000 naira of interest. A processing fee of 2 percent, 4,000 naira, is taken at the start.
So the total cost of borrowing is 64,000 naira, about 10,700 naira a month.
From her records, the bulk stock should add about 12,000 naira a month to her net profit.
That leaves only about 1,300 naira a month, and a slow month would turn it into a loss. So she saves through her cooperative for three months, then borrows a smaller amount from it at lower cost.
Always get the total repayment in writing, and check it fits your monthly profit.
Finance scams
Three warning signs
Real grants never ask you to pay a fee to receive the money.
Be wary of lenders who want your phone contacts. Check FCCPC's approved list.
Never share them. Check a lender is licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria.
Watch for three warning signs. First, real grants never ask you to pay processing or registration fees to receive money.
Second, be wary of loan apps that want your phone contacts. Some abuse borrowers' contacts. Check the FCCPC list of approved digital lenders.
Third, nobody genuine needs your BVN, PIN or OTP. Check that any lender is licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria.
Worked example
Comfort splits her monthly profit
For example, Comfort sells provisions in Calabar and makes about ₦80,000 net profit a month.
Personal pay
Reserve
Growth money

Here is a worked example. Comfort sells provisions in Calabar and makes about 80,000 naira net profit a month. She splits it into three parts and writes the split down.
40,000 naira personal pay, 15,000 for her reserve, and 25,000 as growth money.
Over three months, her growth money buys 75,000 naira of extra stock in her three fastest items, so she stops running out.
Customers ask for frozen chicken, so she buys only what is pre-ordered on WhatsApp. Once demand is proven, she buys a second-hand freezer, without a loan.
Ready to grow?
Signs and safeguards
Ready when
3 to 6 months of net profit
Best sellers often run out
A cash reserve and good records
Do not depend on
One supplier
One big customer
Loose credit to other traders
You are ready to grow when you have made a net profit for three to six months in a row, your best sellers often run out, and you have a reserve and up-to-date records.
As you grow, protect the business. Keep at least two suppliers for your main items, do not let one big buyer become most of your sales, and control credit, because it can drain your cash fast.

Word of mouth, referrals and a neat display
Confirm payments in your own app
Ask for the total repayment in writing
Never pay to receive a grant
Split profit: pay, reserve, growth

To remember. Grow word of mouth with a neat display and referrals. Confirm every payment in your own app. Ask for the total repayment in writing. Never pay to receive a grant. And split your profit into pay, reserve and growth money.
